summary: Specifies the encoding of CCNx messages in a TLV packet format, including TLV types for each message element and the value encodings. Semantics follow the CCNx Semantics specification. It comes from the Information Centric Networking research group and is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8609 specifies how CCNx messages are encoded as packets and nested type-length-value fields. Its fixed-size type and length fields make packet contents easier for forwarders to parse consistently.

questions: what is an interest in ccnx
subtitle: The packet layout and TLV encodings used for CCNx requests and content objects.

tldr.problem: CCNx forwards requests by hierarchical name, so every forwarder must parse message encodings and check request restrictions. The protocol needs an unambiguous wire format.
tldr.mechanism: Packets use an 8-byte fixed header and nested type-length-value fields with fixed 2-byte Type and Length fields. Optional validation fields can carry an integrity check, MAC, or signature.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8609 is an Experimental IRTF document, not an IETF standard. It has been updated by RFC 9510, and the RFC says the specification may change.

today: RFC 8609 is an Experimental IRTF document, not an IETF standard, and was updated by RFC 9510. The RFC says the specification may change and may not suit every application.

sections.title: The CCNx Encoding Specification
sections.content:
CCNx uses hierarchical names to forward requests and match responses; it does not use endpoint addresses for this purpose. RFC 8569 defines message semantics, while RFC 8609 defines their packet and value encodings.

The document defines a Type-Length-Value (TLV) scheme with fixed 2-byte Type and 2-byte Length fields. It covers packet formats, message types, values, and the top-level types used by Interests and Content Objects. Type numbers are interpreted in their enclosing context.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines the bytes used to represent CCNx packets and messages. Another RFC defines what those messages mean and how the protocol operates.

sections.title: Packet Structure and Fixed Header
sections.content:
A CCNx packet begins with an 8-byte fixed header, followed by optional hop-by-hop headers and a packet payload. The payload contains the CCNx message and may include validation fields. Because the payload is self-sufficient, a network stack can discard the outer headers and still process the message.

The fixed header identifies the packet version and type and gives packet and header lengths. An Interest also carries a HopLimit of up to 255; each node decrements it, and a node must not forward an Interest whose decremented value is zero. An Interest Return changes the packet type and adds a return code without adding bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet starts with an 8-byte header that identifies its type and length. An Interest also has a counter that limits how far it can travel.

sections.title: Nested TLVs and Hop-by-Hop Fields
sections.content:
Each TLV contains a 2-byte Type, a 2-byte Length, and a value. The length counts only the value and may be zero. TLVs can be nested, and a type value can have a different meaning in different containers. Types from 0x1000 to 0x1FFF are reserved for experimental use.

Hop-by-hop fields are unordered and may change as a packet travels. The RFC defines Interest Lifetime, Recommended Cache Time, and Message Hash fields. The cache time is guidance, while an ExpiryTime inside a message must be obeyed. Message Hash is unprotected and is useful only within a trusted domain.
sections.plainLanguage: A TLV labels a value and gives its length, and TLVs can be placed inside other TLVs. Some optional outer fields can change as the packet moves through the network.

sections.title: Interests, Names, and Content Objects
sections.content:
The CCNx Message TLV carries an Interest or Content Object. It begins with a message type and length, followed by a Name TLV and optional message fields and payload. An Interest may include a key identifier or content-object hash restriction to narrow which response can satisfy it.

A Name is a sequence of segments. The zero-length Name represents ccnx:/, the default route. Content Objects may specify a payload type and an expiry time; if the payload type is absent, Data is assumed. The RFC also assigns 4096 application-specific name segment types.
sections.plainLanguage: The message contains a name and may contain extra rules for choosing a response. A returned content object can identify its payload type and when it expires.

sections.title: Message Validation
sections.content:
An Interest or Content Object may include a ValidationAlgorithm TLV and a ValidationPayload TLV. The first identifies how to check the message, while the second carries the result, such as a CRC32C value, HMAC, or signature. The protected range includes the message TLV and ValidationAlgorithm TLV.

The RFC defines CRC32C, HMAC-SHA256, RSA-SHA256, and two elliptic-curve signature types. It does not define an encryption envelope or a method for establishing trust in keys; applications handle key trust. The RFC warns that costly signatures on Interests can create a denial-of-service risk and that signatures alone do not prevent replay.
sections.plainLanguage: A message can carry a check, a shared-key code, or a signature so a receiver can validate it. Applications still need to decide which keys to trust and how to prevent replay.

sections.title: Security and Encoding Risks
sections.content:
The RFC uses fixed-size Type and Length fields to prevent multiple encodings of the same value. Without this rule, each forwarder would need to validate alternate encodings and packet filters would become more complex. CCNx names use binary matching, so inconsistent handling of case or URI normalization can also create phishing risks.

Interest Returns have no authenticator from the previous hop, so their payload should be used only to match a local Interest. Caches must follow RFC 8569 rules to avoid serving poisoned content. The document is experimental and may change.
sections.plainLanguage: Fixed-size fields reduce ambiguity when routers read packets. Applications and caches still need rules for checking names, validation data, and returned content.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: No flags are defined; MUST be 0.

fields.name: Header Length
fields.desc: Fixed header plus hop-by-hop headers; minimum 8.
